https://www.dw.com/en/dw-users-on-life-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JTXK Many DW social media users paint a bleak picture of life in Russia Image: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Fuel shortages are disrupting daily routines. Discontent over pay is rising as job prospects weaken. Planning for the future has given way to short-term coping as anxiety spreads in Russia. Even Russia's major pollsters, including state-run VCIOM and FOM, as well as the independent Levada Center, report a clear decline in public sentiment. The Kremlin , however, insists that conditions remain stable. DW invited its social media users to share their stories. All responses have been anonymised for safety reasons. 'If there is gas at all, there are massive queues of 50 to 100 cars' A DW subscriber in Moscow's Pechatniki district described a recent attempt to refuel late at night, covering around 40 kilometers (24 miles) in search of stations with supply. "If there is gas anywhere at all, there's a massive queue of 50 to 100 cars," he said. "We decided that waiting until 3 or 4 a.m. only to head straight to work was a terrible idea, so we went home to sleep. We're on half a tank for now, but by the end of the week we'll either have to hunt for fuel or stand still. Lately, we use the car almost exclusively for trips to the dacha to see our elderly parents." "Now you have to hunt for gas at night. You don't always get lucky. Often there's no gas at all. If there is, it's a two-to-three-hour wait," said another subscriber. Fuel shortage in Russia: Drivers wait in line for gas at a gas station in Moscow Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS Fuel shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have become a leading public grievance. Data from BenZinMap, a fuel tracking portal, show severe sales restrictions across 66 regions as of August 27, with another 16 reporting localized disruptions or sharp price increases. Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), told news portal RBC that refining capacity has fallen by nearly a third, a view echoed by independent analysts. Government measures — including export bans, increased imports, and relaxed fuel-quality standards — have failed to close the gap. The data provided by Russia's state statistics service Rosstat show average retail gasoline prices are up 7.4% this year, outpacing overall inflation of 4.19%. But the averages conceal sharp regional variation. Stations owned by major oil companies have kept price increases relatively modest, drawing long queues. Independent stations are charging significantly more, adding pressure on household budgets. There are few signs of outright panic, though. Drivers appear to be adapting to intermittent supply. "Gas is tight, but St. Petersburg is still holding up for now," said one user. "There were disruptions with gas, but the situation is better now, though it's not available everywhere," said another. Putin faces falling popularity as Russian economy slows To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 'Getting a new job is becoming harder' Official statistics point to exceptionally low unemployment in Russia, with Rosstat reporting a record-low rate of 2.2%. But the figure is misleading. Recruitment platforms hh.ru and SuperJob report a sharp rise in CVs alongside a decline in job postings, suggesting growing dissatisfaction among workers but limited alternatives. Wage growth has also slowed. Companies in struggling sectors such as automaking and coal mining are increasingly shifting staff to reduced hours or mandatory leave. Some DW readers also describe a labor market under strain. "Getting a new job is becoming harder and harder: There are no new openings, and the ones available are either low-paying or involve gruelling 12-hour shifts," wrote one subscriber. "Wage delays make it hard to keep up with loan payments," said another. "I've been working for two-thirds of my salary all summer. It covers food and gym, and that's about it," noted a third. "Layoffs have hit many industries," added a fourth. "The race of inflated salaries is over. And life has gotten monstrously more expensive than before 2022." This grim sentiment has spread even to prestigious white-collar roles. An IT professional from St. Petersburg described the shift: "There are no sudden economic shocks, just a gradual decline that has been dragging on for the last 10 years. Job prospects are tight, and finding a new role will be extremely difficult." A 54-year-old Moscow entrepreneur recalled running a service firm for Western clothing brands before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine . After major clients pulled out, he was forced to close the business. He later launched a new venture manufacturing apparel in Central Asia and Bangladesh for sale on Russian online marketplaces. Early on, rising consumer incomes drove rapid growth. But as economic pressure mounted, conditions worsened. DW users complain about rising prices across Russia Image: Erik Romanenko/TASS/dpa/picture alliance "At first, sales grew faster than we expected. But this business too got caught in the fallout of current policies, isolation, and economic instability," the businessman explained. "Revenues are collapsing catastrophically. And it's not just us. People are cutting back on almost everything." 'People plan nothing, withdraw cash, and buy dollars' The dominant theme in responses received by DW is the absence of a positive vision of the future. Respondents, judging from their comments, are not preparing for a single shock, but for a prolonged period of stagnation or decline. "In our region, the changes are not yet significant," wrote a woman from Sakhalin, an island in Russia's Far East. "Prices are rising, of course, but overall, it feels like people live just as they did before. Personally, the changes in daily life I feel most are with internet service. It has gotten slower, and the VPN is on almost constantly to bypass censorship. A huge number of people from my personal bubble left Russia, though that has been happening since 2022. We sent our son to another country, too." When planning becomes difficult, day-to-day coping dominates. "Fuel shortages, drone attacks... Basic trips to Turkey have become unaffordable," said another subscriber. "People plan nothing, withdraw cash, and buy dollars. There are no hopes for a bright future or a change of power. Everyone lives for today. Drinking has increased significantly — even in Moscow." Beyond anxiety and apathy, a notable number of responses point to growing social fragmentation, with people withdrawing into narrower circles and avoiding broader discussion. "People are mad as hell and blame the West for all their troubles. Life has become far poorer, duller, and more dangerous than before the war," noted one subscriber. "People either shut down or cut off any conversation about life and the war immediately. Almost no one is left putting on a brave face or posturing." "The issue isn't just fuel or the internet — it's the change in people, even quite decent ones," wrote another subscriber, a woman working in healthcare. "There's internal fear, deep irritation — even among those who understand nothing and want to know nothing. But everyone sees the prices. It frightens people. Internal social taboos are vanishing... The intelligentsia suddenly lost its dust, its cultural veneer — especially military-industrial engineers." https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/22/kyiv.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced that Kyiv and Washington want to see the war in Ukraine end "before winter" following what he described as a "positive" meeting with his US counterpart Donald Trump.Zelenskyy and Trump met on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, where the Ukrainian leader said they had discussed potentially "de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy.""I just had a positive and productive meeting with President Trump," he wrote in a post on social media. "Both the U.S. and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter".He added that he and Trump had also spoken about a winter air defence package for Ukraine as well as "other bilateral and multilateral issues."Russia has kept up an almost relentless bombardment of Ukrainian cities and regions since launching its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022, but it has particularly sought to target Ukraine's energy infrastructure over winter periods.Ukraine has also targeted the Russian energy sector as part of its deep strike campaign, which aims to degrade a key driver of the Russian economy and impact the Kremlin's war machine.Ukrainian forces have launched frequent strikes against oil facilities including refineries, terminals, and depots as part of this strategy. Earlier on Tuesday, Zelenskyy announced that one oil refinery had been hit in Bashkortostan and another in the Samara region over the past 24 hours.Speaking to the press together with Zelenskyy in New York, Trump addressed Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, saying they had been a "very serious hit" on Russia but also "a serious hit on the price of diesel."Trump said on Monday that Russia had "unfortunately lost control of its diesel oil industry due to its war with Ukraine" while calling for what he described as the "ridiculous and never ending" war to come to an end."A large number of their diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission," he wrote in a post on his Truth Social account. "The whole world suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!"Zelenskyy responded by insisting that Ukraine was willing to halt strikes on Russia's energy industry if Moscow agreed to do the same."Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part. Solutions are possible," he wrote on X.

Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/Kremlin pool/EPA Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy says more North Koreans to be deployed in Russia Putin’s order comes as both Russian and Ukrainian forces suffer mounting casualties. What we know on day 1,679 Guardian staff and agencies Mon 28 Sep 2026 20.43 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 20.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian president Vladimir Putin has ordered ⁠an increase ​in the size ⁠of the army to 1.55 ⁠million ​active ‌servicemen , according ‌to a ‌presidential decree on Monday. The order comes as both Russia and Ukraine suffer mounting casualties in the more than four-and-a-half-year Ukraine war. The expansion, which follows a similar increase ordered in August, ‌will put the size ​of Russia’s armed forces at ⁠2,441,630. Of those are 1,550,000 ​active ​servicemen, an increase of ​15,500. Ukrainian president ⁠Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ​on X ​on ‌Monday ‌there were now more than 8,000 ‌North Korean ​troops on ⁠Russian territory ​and preparations ​were ​under way ​to ‌deploy ​another ​10,000 troops . Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un confirmed for the first time last year that North Korea had sent troops to fight for Russia in the war with Ukraine, with both leaders describing the soldiers as “heroes”. Citing “new data” on the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, ⁠Zelenskyy said they were “being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia ”. North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 ⁠troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, ​according to Ukrainian ​and South Korean estimates, ​with most deployed in the Kursk region to ​help repel a ‌Ukrainian incursion. Explosions ⁠were heard in the Ukrainian capital of ⁠Kyiv early ⁠on ​Tuesday, a Reuters witness said, as Russia ⁠continues its near-daily attacks. Missile ‌debris fell in the ‌courtyard of a residential building, among other damage, and a non-residential building caught fire in another ‌part of the city, Kyiv mayor ​Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. On Monday, Zelenskyy said nine ⁠people had been killed and more ​than ​80 injured ​in Russian drone strikes ​throughout ‌the country, ​including ​in Kyiv. Pope Leo urged Russia and ⁠Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end their war , hours after ⁠he had urged ⁠European leaders ​seeking to end conflicts to make concessions to achieve peace. Addressing a press conference aboard his ​flight to Rome on Monday after ‌a four-day trip ‌to France, Leo said the 1.4-billion-member Catholic church had an obligation ‌to call for peace and respect of human life. “The Church has a responsibility to promote these values, continually inviting leaders – from Russia and Ukraine, as well as other countries – to come together, sit down, engage ‌in dialogue,” the pope said. Nato’s top military commander said Russia’s sabotage campaign in Europe was failing to put countries off supporting Ukraine . “State-directed sabotage is growing increasingly brazen,” US general Alexus Grynkewich told a committee of EU lawmakers on Monday. Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe cited recent incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport and a Russian naval ship firing flares at a Danish helicopter. “These are clear examples of attempts to instil fear and fracture our unified support to Ukraine. It isn’t working,” he said. Ukraine will postpone some spending commitments, including reconstruction work, because of delays in receiving aid from its foreign backers , Ukraine’s prime minister said. The government would carry out these projects eventually, “but for now, all resources must be directed toward critical areas”, Sergiy Koretsky said on Telegram on Monday. Russia’s offensive has battered Ukraine’s economy, causing billions of dollars in destruction and punching a huge hole in its neighbour’s finances. Putin has ordered the Russian assets of German retailer Metro AG to be placed under temporary administration , amid Russian-German tensions over the Ukraine war. The order, posted on Monday on the government website, did not state a reason. The step follows similar steps against the Russia businesses of global food company Nestlé and French retailer Auchan under a 2023 decree aimed at businesses associated with “unfriendly countries”. Temporary administration has led to local owners taking over the Russia businesses of French dairy concern Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg at knockdown prices. A Russian jet-powered drone struck a Ukrainian village near the Polish border earlier on Monday, damaging a border checkpoint, a regional Ukrainian official said. The official did not give details about the nature of the checkpoint or extent of damage from the blast. Russia has launched multiple attacks near Ukraine’s border with Poland in recent weeks, drawing condemnation from Warsaw and its European allies.
